course: AP Statistics — experimental design and inference — carried through a running clinical trial, with the trial methodology of an introductory clinical epidemiology course
curriculum: Why a comparison needs a control arm at all
Randomisation: what chance assignment buys, and what it cannot buy
Allocation concealment: protecting the moment of entry
Blinding, and the several people it can fail for separately
Block and stratified randomisation: balance in small numbers
Eligibility criteria, and what widening them changes
The recruitment funnel: screened, eligible, consented, entered
The primary endpoint, named in advance, and everything else
Hard endpoints against judged ones, and blinded adjudication
Measurement error, rater drift and inter-rater agreement
Surrogate outcomes, and what they stand in for
Protocol deviations: what they do to the comparison
Amendments and prespecification: a plan that can be dated
Sample size and statistical power
Event-driven trials, and information fraction as progress
Type I and type II error, and what α and β are for
Multiplicity: every extra look and every extra slice costs something
Subgroup analysis, and why a subgroup finding is a hypothesis
Interim analysis, alpha spending and stopping boundaries
Conditional power and futility
The monitoring committee and the firewall around it
Intention to treat against per-protocol
Missing data, and why it matters why it is missing
Effect measures: relative risk, absolute risk reduction, number needed to treat
Confidence intervals: what a point estimate does not say
p-values, and what significance is not
Safety monitoring: adverse events, seriousness and expedited reporting
Causality assessment, and why reporting does not wait for it
Unblinding an individual for their own care
Data cleaning, queries and the database lock
Reporting honestly: what a sentence claims beyond its evidence
External evidence, replication and how a new result is weighed
Consent, and the obligations a trial keeps to the people in it

equations.about: absolute risk reduction — the difference the treatment made
symbols: absolute risk reduction, a difference between two proportions
proportion of the control arm that had the event
proportion of the treatment arm that had the event

equations.about: number needed to treat, and why it is the honest headline
symbols: number of people who must be treated for one to avoid the event
absolute risk reduction, as a fraction rather than a percentage

equations.about: relative risk, and why it hides how big the effect is
symbols: relative risk, a ratio with no units
event rate in the treatment arm
event rate in the control arm

equations.about: a confidence interval, and what its width says
symbols: the interval the result is reported as, rather than a single number
the point estimate the trial measured
the multiplier that makes it a 95 per cent interval

equations.about: why precision improves only as the square root of the sample
symbols: standard error of a measured proportion
number of people it was measured on

equations.about: information fraction — how far through an event-driven trial is
symbols: how many primary endpoint events have been adjudicated so far
the event count the trial was powered on

equations.e: P(at least one false positive) = 1 − (1 − α)^k
equations.about: multiplicity — what testing k things costs
symbols: the error rate allowed for a single test, usually 0.05
how many independent tests were run
chance that at least one of them clears the line by luck alone

equations.about: alpha spending — a budget for error that does not refill
symbols: the error rate consumed by each look at the endpoint
the total error rate the whole trial is allowed, fixed in advance

equations.about: how many events a trial has to see to answer its question
symbols: primary endpoint events required, not participants
the false-positive tolerance, 1.96 at five per cent
the false-negative tolerance, 0.84 at eighty per cent power
the hazard ratio the trial is powered to detect

equations.e: conditional power = P(significant at the end | data so far)
equations.about: what a futility forecast is, and what it is not
symbols: chance the trial reaches significance if it runs to completion
everything observed up to the interim look
the effect size the remainder is assumed to run at — usually the one originally planned
